content: Infantile cortical hyperostosis, also known as Caffey disease, is a self-limiting inflammatory condition that affects infants. It is characterized by changes in the bones, swelling of soft tissues, and irritability. The condition may be present at birth or develop shortly thereafter. The exact cause of the disease remains unknown, and it can occur in both familial and sporadic forms. Infants with this condition typically exhibit a triad of symptoms: soft-tissue swelling, bone lesions, and irritability. The swelling appears suddenly, is deep and firm, and may be tender to the touch. Bone lesions are often asymmetrical and can involve multiple skeletal sites, including the mandible (lower jaw), tibia, ulna, clavicle, scapula, ribs, humerus, femur, fibula, skull, ilium, and metatarsals. When the mandible is affected, infants may refuse to eat, which can result in failure to thrive. The diagnosis of infantile cortical hyperostosis is primarily based on physical examination. X-rays are used to confirm the presence of bone changes and soft-tissue swelling. A biopsy of the affected areas can reveal characteristic histopathological changes. Although there are no specific blood tests for this condition, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and alkaline phosphatase levels are commonly observed. A complete blood count may show anemia (low red blood cell count) and leukocytosis (high white blood cell count). Additional tests may be performed to rule out other conditions. Prenatal cases can sometimes be diagnosed using ultrasound imaging. Differential diagnosis is critical, as other conditions can mimic the symptoms of infantile cortical hyperostosis. Osteomyelitis, a bone infection that requires urgent treatment, must be excluded. Other conditions to consider include physical trauma, child abuse, vitamin A toxicity, hyperphosphatemia, prostaglandin E1 and E2 administration, scurvy, infections (such as syphilis), Ewing sarcoma, and metastatic neuroblastoma. In the early stages of the disease, biopsy findings reveal inflammation of the periosteum (the membrane covering bones) and adjacent soft tissues. As the inflammation resolves, the periosteum remains thickened, and subperiosteal immature lamellar bone is observed, with vascular fibrous tissue occupying the bone marrow spaces. Over time, the inflammation and subperiosteal changes subside, and hyperplasia of lamellar cortical bone becomes evident. Radiographs initially show layers of periosteal new bone formation and cortical thickening. The periosteal new bone may encase the diaphysis of the bone, increasing its diameter. Eventually, the density of the periosteal new bone becomes uniform with the underlying cortex, and the bone remodels to regain a normal appearance. The prognosis for infantile cortical hyperostosis is favorable, as it is a self-limiting condition that typically resolves on its own within 6 to 9 months. Long-term complications, such as deformities of the affected bones, bony fusions, or limb-length discrepancies, are rare but possible. Epidemiologically, the disease affects approximately 3 per 1,000 infants under 6 months of age in the United States. There is no established predilection based on race or sex. Most cases occur by the age of 5 months. The familial form of the disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner with variable penetrance, while the sporadic form has an average onset age of 9 to 11 weeks. The condition was first described in 1945 by John Caffey, who identified a group of infants presenting with tender soft-tissue swelling and cortical thickening of the skeleton, with symptoms appearing within the first three months of life.
